# Risks: releases and updating

Known hazards in how Layover is released and how it updates itself. Part of the
[risks](risks.md), whose numbering this file shares.

---

### 14. Release pipeline trust

**Severity: low. Mostly mitigated.**

The release workflow holds `contents: write` and the Pages workflow holds `id-token: write`. Any
action running in those jobs runs with those tokens, so a compromised upstream would be a
release-pipeline compromise.

*Mitigation:* `.github/workflows/release.yml` is **generated by [`dist`](https://opensource.axo.dev/cargo-dist/)**
and uses only first-party `actions/*` — the three third-party actions the hand-rolled workflow
needed are gone, which was the larger exposure. In `ci.yml` and `pages.yml`, which are still
hand-written, third-party actions are pinned to full commit SHAs.

*Residual, accepted:* the generated workflow interpolates `github.ref_name` into one `run:` block,
which is the injection shape the hand-rolled workflow was fixed for. Exploiting it needs the
ability to push a `v*` tag — the workflow never runs on `pull_request` — so it is a
privileged-user issue rather than an external one. It is **not** patched locally: the file is
generated, `dist plan` would report a hand-edit as drift, and diverging from upstream to fix a
low-severity issue costs more than it saves. Revisit if `dist` addresses it upstream.

*Residual:* `actions/*` are pinned to major tags, which is the usual trade-off.

### 26. Layover now makes a request of its own

**What could happen.** Every running factory with `[update] mode = "notify"` — the default — asks
github.com once a day for the newest release's manifest. That request carries the machine's address
and a `User-Agent` of `layover/<version>`: GitHub learns that a Layover of that version runs there. On
a network that must not reach out, it is a request nobody expected, and a proxy may log or refuse it.
What is read back steers nothing yet — it is only shown — but a manifest is input from the network,
and the next step, applying a release, makes it load-bearing.

**Why it is accepted.** The alternative is a factory that runs a release with a known fault for
weeks because nobody looked; the request names nothing about the factory, its agents or its work.
It is one request for a public file, on github.com rather than the rate-limited API, so a building
of factories behind one NAT does not spend each other's budget. No telemetry is sent, and none is
planned while the maintainer is the only user.

**Mitigation.** `LAYOVER_UPDATE=off` stops every request on a machine, whatever a factory says, and
`[update] mode = "off"` stops one factory's. A failed check is retried with back-off and never fails
a run, a start or a validation. The manifest is parsed with every field optional and size-capped at
2 MB; a manifest naming no version is refused; nothing in it is executed or rendered as HTML.
`LAYOVER_UPDATE_SOURCE` points a site at a mirror it controls.

### 27. A release's provenance is only as good as `gh` and its pins

**What could happen.** A staged release is trusted to run, and in time to install, because `gh
attestation verify` said Layover's release workflow built it from its tag. If `gh` were replaced on
`PATH` by something that always exits 0, every archive would read as verified. If the pins were
wrong — another repository's workflow, another tag — a release built elsewhere could pass. And on a
machine without `gh`, nothing is verified at all.

**Why it is accepted.** The alternative, verifying inside the binary, was tried and the library
refused genuine bundles and skipped the transparency-log proof (see the decision log). `gh` is
GitHub's own verifier, and something that can replace it on `PATH` can already replace `layover`.

**Mitigation.** The pins are constants, tested: repository, signer workflow, `refs/tags/<tag>`,
issuer and predicate. The archive must also match the manifest's SHA-256 and the `.sha256` file, and
the binary must then say it is the version and platform it should be. A release whose provenance
could not be checked is downloaded but never run, never installed unattended, and installed by hand
only with `--trust-checksum-only`, which is said in the record.

### 28. Installing a release restarts the Tower, and a release can fail in ways a test does not

**What could happen.** An install cuts off any run still alive at `[update] max_drain`, and a run
cut off halfway through an external effect repeats it when recovery restarts it — the hazard of
risk 17, at a moment a person chose rather than a crash. A release can pass every check and still
be wrong: healthy by the Tower's measure, and failing runs that used to pass. Under systemd or
launchd, a new binary that dies before it reads the handover never counts a start, so it is never
rolled back automatically; the service manager restarts it until it gives up. And a Tower started by
an update writes what it prints to `.layover/serve.log`, not to the terminal or log the old one
wrote to, which a person looking in the old place will not find.

**Why it is accepted.** Not updating is the larger hazard for a factory nobody watches, and every
one of these is bounded: the deadline waits out the longest `timeout` by default, `recovery =
"manual"` agents postpone it rather than being cut off, nothing installs without a person asking,
and nothing is installed that was not verified and did not validate the factory.

**Mitigation.** The replaced binary is kept for `keep_previous` (a week), and `layover update
rollback` puts it back. On Windows the old Tower supervises the new one and rolls back a release
that does not answer within two minutes, at once. `doctor` says when a rollback happened in the last
thirty days, and `layover update log` keeps every install, refusal, postponement and rollback.

### 29. An unattended install takes a release nobody has looked at

**What could happen.** Under `[update] mode = "auto"`, a factory installs a patch or minor release
by itself. A release can be wrong in a way no check here sees — healthy, validating the factory, and
quietly worse at the work — and every unattended factory takes it once its cool-off has passed.

**Why it is accepted.** It is opt-in, per factory: the default only tells. And a factory nobody
watches that never updates runs on known faults.

**Mitigation.** The cool-off — a day for a patch, two for a minor — is the time to withdraw a bad
release: marking it a pre-release on GitHub moves `releases/latest` back, and a fixed patch follows.
A major release, a layout change, an unverified release and one that gives a new warning all wait
for a person. Installs happen only in the `window` chosen, or when the factory has been idle. Every
one is logged, the bell rings for it, the previous binary is kept a week, and `layover update
rollback` puts it back.
